/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.headline: Healey urged to offer energy support in budget as bills rise 4%
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.excerpt: John Healey is under growing pressure to offer fresh energy support for households in next month’s budget as millions face a 4% rise in charges from Thursday to an average of £1,723 a year for a typical home. In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool this week, the chancellor warned that the government had limited resources to cushion the worldwide economic shocks hitting Britain, while arguing his budget would have fiscal discipline at its core. The quarterly energy price cap, set by the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will rise to its highest level in three years despite Andy Burnham’s decision to cut VAT from electricity bills to save the average household £45 a year from 1 October. Households also face rising road fuel costs after diesel prices reached a record high of almost £2 a litre this week, which is expected to accelerate the rising cost of goods across the economy. Treasury sources insist the 28 October budget will be tightly focused amid the challenging global backdrop, as bond market jitters add to the pressure on the public finances. Insiders said tax devolution was likely to be centre stage to meet Andy Burnham’s promise to shake up Whitehall, while several big decisions could be pushed back to a spending review next year. Some MPs are privately concerned that Healey and his team have failed to grasp the severity of the energy crunch ahead. “Without it [fresh energy support], the vibes will end,” said one Labour MP.
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.trail: Millions of people in Great Britain face increase from Thursday to an average of £1,723 a year for a typical home

/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.headline: Energy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulating
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.excerpt: Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill forecast to jump by £276 to the equivalent of nearly £2,000 year. It is a worrying outlook but there are practical steps you can take to mitigate the predicted price shock. Fixed energy deals “Switching energy tariff to a well-priced fixed deal is the biggest lever households on the price cap can pull to bring their costs down right now,” says Richard Neudegg, the director of regulation at Uswitch. About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable tariffs set by Ofgem’s price cap, which increases by 4% from Thursday, equivalent to taking the typical annual dual-fuel bill up by £60 to £1,723. The cap is due to rise 16% further to £1,999 in January, according to the latest forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight. “The cheapest deal on the market is currently £324 less than this,” says Neudegg. The number of cap-beating deals has been steadily declining in recent weeks but there are still 34 deals below the January forecast, with some cheaper than October’s rates. At the moment the cheapest is Fuse Energy’s 12-month fix at £1,675, beating the October price cap by £48, and potentially January’s by as much as £324. Check your boiler and hot water settings Combi boilers work best when they heat radiators to 60C or below. But in many homes the “flow temperature” is often set much too high at 70C- 80C.
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.trail: The price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to save

/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.headline: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.excerpt: Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach almost £2,000 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter. The government’s cap on energy prices is poised to jump by 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight. The latest blow to struggling households was published as millions braced for energy charges to rise by 4% from Thursday as the quarterly energy bill cap climbs to its highest level in three years this winter. The consultancy’s January forecast increase is well above its previous prediction of a 9% rise, with analysts blaming the uptick on the recent rise in gas market prices to three-year highs. It would be the biggest quarterly jump since January 2023, when the energy crisis that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine the year before was at its height. Craig Lowrey, a principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas, and now they face the biggest price cap rise we’ve seen in four years.” The chief executive of the supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, said the UK was “walking into a second energy crisis”.
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.trail: Cap poised to rise by 16% to equivalent of £1,999 for dual-fuel bill, the biggest quarterly increase since January 2023

/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.headline: What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?
/money/2026/oct/06/chancellor-plans-majo.excerpt: Andy Burnham’s first address to the Labour party conference as prime minister addressed Britain’s rising energy costs and sluggish economic growth with plans for a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid. The proposals to set up Great British Grid, first revealed by the Guardian, build on the party’s manifesto pledge to create Great British Energy, a state-owned company to invest in renewables. However, GB Grid faces a tougher challenge: lowering bills and supercharging the economy through public investment in the electricity network. “We have a cost crisis. We all know it,” Burnham argues. “The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. “We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.” Few would disagree with the diagnosis – but is direct government investment in grids the remedy Britain needs? What is the grid plan? Burnham says the government-owned GB Grid will work with the private sector and network companies to increase competition in the sector, drive down costs and speed up delivery. This should help companies and businesses connect to the power grid sooner, and make energy costs cheaper for all consumers. The creation of GB Grid is timely.

The prime minister will use his first speech as party leader to announce the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid. In a speech focusing heavily on undoing what the prime minister calls “40 years of neoliberalism”, he will promise greater public control of energy, water and housing. He is also set to lay out more details on how he will pay for his pledge to create a national care service, with senior ministers refusing to rule out scrapping the pensions triple lock after the next election to free funding. Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether. Burnham will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We have a cost crisis. We all know it. The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. “We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.” He will add: “Within 10 years, I want our energy costs to be in line with other nations in Europe.

/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.headline: New UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF boss
/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.excerpt: New oil and gas projects are a “no-brainer” that pose “no contradiction” to the net zero agenda, according to the head of EDF Energy. Simone Rossi has joined a string of renewables leaders in making the case for more North Sea production as the government prepares to decide on two projects there. He said ministers should give the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields the green light, while accelerating support for heat pumps and electric vehicles. “It will take decades to wean off from that dependency,” Rossi said in an interview with the BBC. “So while this is happening we should use the resources that we’ve got rather than importing them from afar. For me, it’s really a no-brainer. It is not in contradiction.” New North Sea developments would help to create jobs and increase government tax receipts that could be used to support households struggling to pay energy bills, according to Rossi. He said locally produced fossil fuels had lower emissions than imports because they do not need to transported over long distances. “In the UK the only way we can reduce emissions is to genuinely reduce the usage of fossil fuels at the point of use,” he said. “Over time, the only solution is electricity.” The boss of EDF Energy, which generates about a fifth of the UK’s low-carbon electricity, has become the latest high-profile advocate of climate action to also make a case for more North Sea production.
/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.trail: Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi

/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.headline: Greens just four points behind Labour in urban areas, poll reveals
/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.excerpt: The Greens are just four points behind Labour in urban constituencies across the UK, putting them within touching distance of taking as many as 40 seats if the result was replicated at the next election, according to new polling by a Labour-linked thinktank. The survey by ThinkLabour, which has extensive links to Andy Burnham’s government, finds that urban voters have moved in large numbers towards the UK’s Green parties since the 2024 general election. The research highlights the challenge Labour faces in holding on to the Holborn and St Pancras seat in the face of a challenge from Zack Polanski, the party leader in England and Wales, at next month’s byelection. The study’s authors warn that evidence from previous electoral battles between the two parties suggests Labour politicians should dial down direct attacks on the Greens for fear of looking as if they are “kicking a puppy”. Christabel Cooper, one of the report’s authors, said: “The previous administration [under Keir Starmer] had always banked on the fact that Labour would be able to say to people who vote Green that they would get Nigel Farage as prime minister. “But in the 40 seats that we have identified, that is no longer the case – the Greens can claim to be the progressives’ party of choice.” She added that evidence from other elections where the party has gone head to head with Labour suggests that progressives dislike aggressive attacks on the Greens.
/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.trail: Exclusive: UK’s Green parties could take 40 seats if result replicated at next election, according to Labour-linked thinktank

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen next week. However, multiple Whitehall sources say the decision is not expected to be made in the remaining few days before the House of Commons goes into recess on Tuesday for party conference season. The delay means the announcement is unlikely to come before Holborn and St Pancras constituents vote in a high-profile byelection on 8 October, in which the Green party leader Zack Polanski is the candidate vying against Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali in Keir Starmer’s former seat. Polanski has criticised the government over signals that it will press ahead with Jackdaw despite the hottest ever summer caused by the climate crisis. After his selection, Polanski said Labour has “started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal”. “They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a byelection where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding. “Labour talks about change, but this is change for the worse.

/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.headline: Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full
/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.excerpt: Zack Polanski has challenged Andy Burnham’s government to publish an unredacted version of an explosive report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of overseas ecosystems would have catastrophic consequences for the UK’s national security. The Green party leader in England said the prime minister should come clean about the scale and impact of the climate and nature crisis and called on the government to publish in full the report that warns the UK faces devastating security consequences. Speaking at the Wild Summit event in Bristol on Wednesday, Polanski asked the prime minister: “Will you tell the truth – and release the full unredacted report from the joint intelligence chiefs? Or will you keep hiding the truth from the public?” The Guardian revealed last year that the report paints a devastating picture of severe food shortages, price rises, migration, political destabilisation and possible war, resulting from the collapse of ecosystems, fuelled by the human-induced climate crisis and over-exploitation. A redacted 14-page version, including some of the report’s findings, was published in January but the government has repeatedly refused to publish the full version, despite repeated freedom of information requests from journalists and calls from MPs.

/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.headline: Zack Polanski announces plans to fight byelection in Keir Starmer’s old seat
/politics/2026/oct/06/labour-figures-rul.excerpt: Zack Polanski has announced his intention to fight for the Commons seat vacated by Keir Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection pitting the mass campaigning of his Greens against a resurgent Labour under Andy Burnham. Local Greens in Holborn and St Pancras still have to formally select their candidate under a process that will not be completed until next Friday. But it seems inevitable they will endorse Polanski, under whose leadership the party has soared in the polls, with membership more than tripling. Polanski told the Camden New Journal newspaper that he wanted to “stand up for people struggling to pay their bills”, adding he was confident that the Greens could win the seat. He lives in east London and had been expected to target a parliamentary seat there. Polanski, who was elected leader of the Greens in England and Wales a year ago, previously lived in Holborn and St Pancras and is a London assembly member. “I know it well and I love it,” he told the newspaper. “It represents so many of the things that make London so special.” The area had “been held back by governments who have failed to make the changes to improve people’s lives”, he added. The Greens are planning to flood the north London constituency with campaigners this weekend, building on the mobilisation model used to overturn a 13,000-plus Labour majority in Greater Manchester’s Gorton and Denton in February.

/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.headline: UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closure
/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.excerpt: The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week. This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel. The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright. Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements. The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.trail: Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements

/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.headline: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family
/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.excerpt: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror. More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in the West Bank village of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire. The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters. Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of Israel’s elections next month. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”. Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.

/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.excerpt: Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of Palestinians they were right that Labour’s approach had not been enough, saying he was heeding the calls of millions of people by imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements. The foreign secretary will tell the Labour party conference that the government will take more explicitly progressive foreign policy positions under Andy Burnham, and that the UK will be a leader among like-minded countries in a new age of diplomacy. He will say there is a “fundamental and wider lesson from Israel and Palestine about how we have changed our approach as a party”, saying Labour will succeed “because of, not in spite of, our progressive values”. He will talk of the start of a new and more muscular foreign policy. “We are not here to accept the status quo but to change it at home and abroad,” he will say. The party’s conference hall was often the scene of fierce opposition to Keir Starmer’s stance on Israel and Palestine in Labour’s final year of opposition and early in government. Since becoming foreign secretary, Miliband has announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 countries – including France and Canada – announcing they would also impose sanctions.

/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.headline: British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins
/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.excerpt: British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months. A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks ago plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements and new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament. The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of as many as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states. Finance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts.

/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.headline: Trump administration again denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly
/world/2026/oct/06/israeli-settlers-beat.excerpt: The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York. The state department said in a statement the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations. “As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said. The move marks the second year in a row the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person. The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against it in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region”.

Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict petrol sales. “Fifty-one per cent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara said. “Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory.” Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact, Vladimir Putin said they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” the Russian president told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts last Thursday. Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for high petrol prices, saying the Iran war was no longer responsible.

/world/2026/oct/06/plague-epidemic-risk-.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says
/world/2026/oct/06/plague-epidemic-risk-.excerpt: Ukraine will increase its attacks on Russian oil refineries, but won’t target civilians, because of a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. Ukraine’s intelligence service has obtained documents showing the Russian ruler, Vladimir Putin, has issued a new doctrine of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, ⁠Ukraine’s president told Reuters. “We saw documents and we know that they ⁠allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals,” he said. “To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation.” “We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But we will not respond, of course … on any civilian objects.” Russian attacks on Saturday in Ukraine killed at least six people and damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, disrupting traffic for a third day in Moscow’s latest effort to complicate life in the Ukrainian capital. Previously, it has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, gas stations, datacentres and other civilian targets.
/world/2026/oct/06/plague-epidemic-risk-.trail: Kyiv working on better jamming capabilities, interceptors for Shahed drones and ballistic missiles that can reach Moscow. What we know on day 1,684

/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.headline: Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.excerpt: The University of Cambridge has asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday. Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career. Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and she sought to defend her institution from criticism. “We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question,” Prentice said. “We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes.” Arday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest ever black professor at the age of 37. Arday denied accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours after the investigation was announced.
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.trail: Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death

/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.headline: Inquest opens into death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.excerpt: A coroner has formally opened an inquest into the death of Jason Arday, who resigned as a professor at the University of Cambridge amid allegations of plagiarism. Arday, 41, died at his home in Battersea, south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation. Family members watched the 10-minute hearing at London inner south coroner’s court via a video link. The senior coroner, Dr Julian Morris, said: “London ambulance service and the Met police attended the home address after he’d been found unresponsive by returning family members. Sadly, despite resuscitative efforts, he was pronounced dead at the scene. The Met police confirmed that the scene was not suspicious.” He said that given the circumstances, he would launch an investigation into Arday’s death, adjourning the inquest until an unspecified later date. Morris also implored the media to be “mindful of your reporting” and to have regard for Arday’s family and the public. There has been an intense debate over media handling of the allegations against Arday, with his family and supporters highly critical of the coverage and others defending it. In a statement announcing his resignation, Arday said he was driven to resign because the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”. Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, when he became the university’s youngest-ever black professor.
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.trail: Academic was found unresponsive by family members, inquest told, as coroner adjourns proceedings to later date

/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.headline: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by his university
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.excerpt: Nathan Cofnas, the academic who made plagiarism allegations against Prof Jason Arday before his death, has been suspended by a university. Arday, 41, resigned from his role at the University of Cambridge this month after coverage of Cofnas’s accusations of plagiarism. The allegations, which were not proven in any formal investigation, triggered questions about Arday’s achievements. There has been stiff criticism of Cambridge over its handling of the affair, but also of the coverage by some media. The university’s chancellor, Chris Smith, described it as a “racist feeding frenzy”. Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, was found dead in Battersea, south London, on Friday. The “American anti-woke” blogger Cofnas is a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University’s department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website. In a post on X on Thursday, Cofnas said: “I am under investigation by my university for discriminating against Arday.” He added in a separate post: “I was just suspended by Ghent University. They will almost certainly fire me.” Ghent University confirmed his suspension after saying they had been “shocked” by Arday’s death and that it “should prompt reflection”, adding that the institution “opposes discrimination, hatred and racism”.
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.trail: Researcher Nathan Cofnas previously claimed Black people would hold few high-profile positions in a meritocracy

/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.headline: Tens of thousands pay tribute to Jason Arday at Trafalgar Square vigil
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.excerpt: Tens of thousands of people gathered in Trafalgar Square in London to remember and pay tribute to Jason Arday, the former Cambridge professor who died on Friday. Stand Up to Racism, which organised the vigil, estimated that 30,000 mourners had gathered in the square to listen to emotional speeches from MPs, friends and campaigners on Arday’s life and legacy and join in a minute’s silence. Many were dressed in black and held flowers, which they were asked to leave beneath Nelson’s column. People also carried placards reading “rest in power”. Arday, 41, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in south London on Friday. He had just resigned from his role as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, after widespread scrutiny over accusations of plagiarism, which he rejected, and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements. Opening the event, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the local MP for Arday’s family in Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “I’m going to look around you and look at how many people have come tonight. “That tells you what Jason meant. He held doors open behind him. He kept them open and thousands of us walked through. That is why this place is full tonight. And I know that all of you are grieving. I know there are many people that aren’t even here.” Ribeiro-Addy asked that people respect the privacy of Arday’s family, who “lost their son, their brother.
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.trail: MPs, friends and campaigners gathered to remember former Cambridge professor after his death on Friday

/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.headline: Support for Jason Arday’s family shows ‘Britain still cares’, says Windrush campaigner
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.excerpt: A Windrush campaigner who launched a fundraiser for Jason Arday’s family has said the outpouring of support shows “Britain still cares”. Arday, who was found dead on Friday, had resigned the previous week from his post as professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge after allegations of plagiarism were made against him. A vigil for the professor, organised by the group Stand Up to Racism, will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. Calls are growing for an investigation into media reporting of the case. An open letter to Andy Burnham demanding a public inquiry “to ensure we never see a tragic death like Dr Arday’s again” has gathered more than 85,000 names. The prime minister is said to be open to the idea and has not ruled out “Leveson 2” – the planned second part of the earlier inquiry into British press standards, which was cancelled in 2018. He has stressed, however, that now is a time for reflection while the usual processes – such as an inquest – are followed and concluded. Earlier, Cambridge’s chancellor, Chris Smith, broke his silence over the controversy and described what he called a “racist feeding frenzy” around the academic’s death. On Saturday, Sir Patrick Vernon, who played a leading role in the successful campaign to establish a national Windrush Day and is also among the letter’s signatories set up a GoFundMe crowdfunding page, which has collected more than £160,000.
/education/2026/oct/06/cambridge-univers.trail: Calls grow for inquiry into media reporting of the case as Cambridge chancellor criticises ‘racist feeding frenzy’

/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.headline: Glasgow city council reaches pay deal with union to avert fire-and-rehire plan
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.excerpt: Glasgow city council has reached an agreement with the trade union Unison over pay and grading, averting one of the UK’s biggest ever fire-and-rehire exercises. Talks between the council and the GMB, Unite and Unison unions previously broke down when Unison refused to ballot its members on a new pay and grading system, designed to resolve historical equal pay issues. The collapse of talks prompted the council to contact 23,000 workers, its entire non-teaching staff, at the end of last month to inform them they were at risk of being dismissed and reappointed, many on less favourable terms. The move led to significant backlash from opposition parties, unions and council employees. The original proposal that led Unison to walk out of negotiations would have resulted in wage cuts for 11% of staff, but on Monday the council agreed to protect their pay for three years. Unison said many issues remained unresolved and that negotiations would continue, but that it would ballot its members this month. The council has agreed to continue negotiating on issues including the equality impacts of the new pay structure. Ricky Bell, the leader of Glasgow city council, said he was “delighted that we have been able to reach agreement with Unison” and “remove the unpalatable prospect of fire-and-rehire”. “This is a strong and fair deal,” he added.
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.trail: ‘Strong and fair’ proposal to be taken to members’ ballot after previous offer led Unison to walk out of negotiations

/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.headline: Thousands of Glasgow council workers face pay cuts in one of UK’s biggest fire-and-rehire plans
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.excerpt: Thousands of Glasgow council workers face being sacked and reappointed under less favourable terms in one of the UK’s biggest ever “fire-and-rehire” exercises, after union negotiations broke down once again this week. About 23,000 workers – all of the council’s non-teaching staff – first heard they were affected last week when talks between the SNP-led council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart. Those negotiations concerned a new pay and grading system designed to resolve historical pay equality issues. Unison refused to ballot its members on an offer that would mean pay cuts for 11% of council employees, prompting the council to begin issuing fire-and-rehire letters. At the beginning of this week the fire-and-rehire plans were temporarily paused when Unison returned to the negotiating table. But when discussions collapsed again midweek, the council’s leader, Ricky Bell, suggested Unison members could still be fired and rehired while negotiations with GMB and Unite continued. Unison said it was seeking advice on the legality of its members being treated differently based on union membership. An emergency motion by Green councillors to block the scheme was also rejected on Thursday by the council’s city administration committee, with the Glasgow Greens co-leader Anthony Carroll saying the city was “facing a genuine cliff-edge of one of the largest fire-and-rehire schemes in the UK being implemented”.
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.trail: Unison union refuses to ballot members on offer that would make 11% of council employees worse off

/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.headline: Man sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.excerpt: A worker fired by the makers of Grand Theft Auto has said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working. Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal in Glasgow examining whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 employees for trade union activity on Friday that he thought the company started keeping an eye on a group of workers after the petition was sent to leadership in 2023. Rockstar, which disputes the claims, says Oram and his colleagues were dismissed for gross misconduct after confidential company information was shared, not because of trade union membership or activity. The workers had been helping to make Grand Theft Auto VI, which is set for release on 19 November and will probably be among the biggest launches in gaming history. The production for the game, which has reportedly generated more than $3bn (£2.27bn) in preorders, is led from the company’s Edinburgh office Rockstar North. Much of the case relies on what was shared in a Discord forum, used by about 300 Rockstar employees to discuss the company. Oram was involved in setting up the forum and helped moderate it, which is where Rockstar says sensitive information was shared and discussed. Oram told the tribunal that discussions on the forum could “get a bit out of hand”. Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar at the tribunal, read Oram the forum rules requiring workers to remain “professional and constructive” when posting.
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.trail: UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity

/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.headline: Where are the Ugandan boxers? Four are latest athletes to vanish after UK sports events
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.excerpt: Years of arduous preparation and training had come to fruition and the pressure was finally lifted. After competing for their country in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, athletes from Uganda were afforded a couple of days’ sightseeing time before catching their plane home on Tuesday. But when the flight took off, there were four empty seats. Only two of the team of six boxers returned to Uganda. Ibrahim Kemis, Emily Nakalema, Angel Katushabe and the captain, Nuhu Batte, were missing. One of the athletes reportedly told the Ugandan news website NBS Sport they were intending to claim asylum in the UK where there are better training facilities. But the team manager for the Ugandan Commonwealth Games team told the BBC he had “absolutely no idea” what basis they would have for an asylum claim in the UK. “It’s nothing political, it’s nothing to do with gender or something [like that] – I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that,” said the team’s chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe. The first indication something was amiss was that their phones were turned off – against the rules of the Ugandan team camp, as athletes need permission to come and go. And then they vanished. The Guardian understands the foursome were initially taken in by a boxing gym in Glasgow but are no longer in Scotland. The owner of the gym did not respond to queries about the missing boxers. Kayangwe hoped they would make the “right decision” and return to Uganda.
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.trail: Team manager has ‘no idea’ why they disappeared, after reports one of Commonwealth Games athletes said they intended to claim asylum

/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.headline: ‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth Games
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.excerpt: The 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow have already provided plenty of highlights. But fans across the world have been dazzled by one particular breakout star: the “mop man”. When a cleaner came out at half-time during a netball match to wipe down the court before the restart, everything appeared normal. But as the cleaner swept, and the first bars of Queen’s I Want to Break Free rang out in the venue, he went from sweeping to a standing split. A full dance routine set to the 1984 hit then followed, much to the surprise and delight of the audience at the OVO Hydro. The crowd watched him do the worm, splits and front handsprings. He has since entertained crowds during breaks in play at a number of other events and clips of his performances have gone viral online. The man behind the mop is CJ Miller, 25, from Livingston, West Lothian, a trained dancer who was hired by the Games to keep crowds entertained during intermissions. He considers himself more of an introvert than his cleaning alter ego. “I’m an anxious and paranoid queen,” said Miller. “And I’m so grateful for the turn of events. It’s been a lovely 50 minutes of fame. I wish I’d had a haircut before it happened.” Miller was initially told he would be part of a flashmob at the Games with other dancers. “Then it was, ‘oh, here’s a mop. Here’s the song.’ It wasn’t until the Tuesday before the Games I found out it was gonna be Boo Boo the Fool here, on his own,” Miller laughed, pointing to himself.
/uk-news/2026/oct/07/scottish-film-till-.trail: CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time routines

/business/2026/oct/07/jaguar-launch-type.headline: Range Rover launches its first electric vehicle, with starting price of £154,070
/business/2026/oct/07/jaguar-launch-type.excerpt: Range Rover has launched its first electric vehicle – a year later than planned – offering a greener option for fans of gargantuan British-made SUVs who are also conscious about the climate crisis. Due to be built in Solihull, the home of the marque since 1970, the vehicle comes with an eye-watering price tag, starting at £154,070. However, the delayed launch marks a milestone departure from cars powered by fossil fuels for Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which is owned by India’s Tata Motors but headquartered in Coventry in the UK. It also provides a much-needed moment of positivity for JLR, which reported falling profits earlier this year as it counted the cost of Donald Trump’s tariff wars and supply chain disruption after a crippling cyber-attack last year. JLR said it had given extra training to 10,500 staff working on the project and that the car had undergone testing equivalent to 38 trips around the world, more than any other Range Rover. The company said the luxury vehicle, which can reach 60mph in 4.3 seconds, heralded “a new era of enhanced refinement and capability”. While the model’s electric powertrain will limit its impact on the environment compared with JLR’s petrol and diesel models, SUVs of its size are consistently linked to higher numbers of road deaths in accidents involving pedestrians.
/business/2026/oct/07/jaguar-launch-type.trail: Fully electric SUV unveiled after year-long delay and will be built at Jaguar Land Rover’s plant in Solihull

/business/2026/oct/07/jaguar-launch-type.headline: UK’s biggest EV battery gigafactory shelves expansion as Jaguar Land Rover talks stall
/business/2026/oct/07/jaguar-launch-type.excerpt: The UK’s biggest gigafactory has shelved plans to expand production in Sunderland because of stalled talks on a deal to supply electric car batteries to Jaguar Land Rover. Chinese-owned AESC produces batteries for Nissan at its gigafactory next door to the Japanese carmaker’s Sunderland plant. However, AESC has had to push back its ramp-up plans because of lower-than-expected demand from Nissan and the lack of a deal with JLR, according to people with knowledge of the situation. The delays are another sign of the slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric cars. Andy Burnham’s Labour government on Friday revealed that it could cut the UK’s electric car sales targets further, in a potential blow to the electric vehicle supply chain. Battery manufacturers in the UK and Europe have had a difficult few years as carmakers have retreated from previous ambitious targets to switch from internal combustion engines to electric vehicles. Several big European battery projects have gone bankrupt, while others have been forced to scale back plans in an industry dominated by Chinese players such as CATL and BYD, the world’s biggest maker of electric cars. JLR’s sister company, Agratas, is building its own gigafactory in Somerset, England. That plant is not scheduled to start production until 2027. The Guardian in June reported that Agratas has faced construction difficulties that could delay the start of production further.
/business/2026/oct/07/jaguar-launch-type.trail: Chinese-owned AESC has pushed back plans in sign of slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric cars
